action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced putaminal DAT binding, right 1.02 and left 1.29 (normal >1.50), worse on the right opposite the worse left side, with preserved caudate binding: presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.label: Order a DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) to separate pure drug-induced parkinsonism from an underlying presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
action_criteria.rationale: Three years of metoclopramide make drug-induced parkinsonism a live alternative, and the history has no other marker of degeneration: the scan is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism and abnormal when a degenerative deficit has been unmasked [Marshall_2009]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Metoclopramide flagged as a central D2 antagonist that opposes levodopa, with prokinetic options free of central D2 blockade; tamsulosin and lisinopril flagged for the standing blood pressure
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for dopamine-blocking drugs and drugs that lower standing blood pressure
action_criteria.rationale: Metoclopramide is a current dopamine-receptor blocker, an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, and tamsulosin and lisinopril will add to any levodopa-related orthostatic fall [Postuma_2015]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not start levodopa while metoclopramide remains in the regimen
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose Parkinson's disease unmasked by metoclopramide: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues, but the abnormal DaTscan shows a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause; confirm that the parkinsonism persists after withdrawal [Postuma_2015][Marshall_2009]

Stop metoclopramide, with the gastroenterologist, and manage the gastroparesis without central D2 blockade (domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short courses of erythromycin), watching his weight
Reassess after withdrawal: drug-induced signs can take weeks to months to resolve; the abnormal DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit that withdrawal will not reverse [Marshall_2009]

Once metoclopramide is stopped, if the parkinsonism persists and limits function, start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), review the response after 2 to 3 months, and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each step because tamsulosin and lisinopril add to orthostatic falls [NICE_NG71]
Refer for physiotherapy for gait and balance with fall-prevention advice (two near-falls on turning, two steps of retropulsion)

No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive feature: CSF has no role in this parkinsonism
No murmur, heart failure or cardiac symptom: an echocardiogram does not inform the parkinsonism
No palpitations, syncope or presyncope: rhythm monitoring is not indicated

differential.key_features: Coexisting contributor: metoclopramide can worsen the signs, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not produce; persistence after withdrawal confirms
Only scattered small periventricular foci and no basal ganglia lacunes; asymmetric upper-limb bradykinesia and rigidity, no stepwise course, asymmetric presynaptic deficit on DaTscan
No cerebellar signs, no urinary incontinence or orthostatic symptoms; normal pons and putamina on MRI
Evans index 0.29 with proportionate sulci; no urinary incontinence; MMSE 28/30; upper-limb parkinsonism
No vertical gaze palsy, no falls, normal midbrain on MRI
No postural or action tremor is described in the history or on examination; bradykinesia with decrement and rigidity are not features of ET

key_clinical_evidence: Bilateral bradykinesia with decrement and cogwheel rigidity, slightly worse on the left, with hypomimia, hypophonia and micrographia; a left-hand tremor at rest is reported by his wife but not seen on examination [Postuma_2015]
Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for 3 years, started before the 12 to 14 month motor history: current D2-blocker exposure is an MDS absolute exclusion while it continues [Postuma_2015]

DaTscan with reduced putaminal binding, right 1.02 and left 1.29 (normal >1.50), opposite the worse left side, with caudate sparing: a presynaptic deficit that pure drug-induced parkinsonism does not cause, and the only marker of degeneration in this case [Marshall_2009]
No dream enactment, no reported smell loss: the history gives no non-motor argument either way
MRI with scattered small periventricular foci and proportionate ventricles (Evans 0.29): no vascular, NPH or atypical-parkinsonism signature
Metoclopramide carries an FDA boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with use beyond 12 weeks

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Metoclopramide can worsen parkinsonism, but the abnormal asymmetric DaTscan shows an underlying presynaptic deficit: the drug unmasks rather than explains the syndrome

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

alternatives: Domperidone 10 mg up to three times daily for the shortest possible time, where available, after an ECG
Ondansetron for nausea (5-HT3 antagonist, no dopamine blockade)
contraindications: Metoclopramide with levodopa or a dopamine agonist: contraindicated in the EU product information (mutual antagonism); metoclopramide is also contraindicated in Parkinson's disease.
interactions: Metoclopramide is a central dopamine D2 receptor antagonist: it causes and worsens parkinsonism and opposes levodopa. For gastroparesis use a prokinetic without central D2 blockade, such as domperidone where available after an ECG for the QTc, or short-term erythromycin.

Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Lisinopril lowers blood pressure and can add to the orthostatic effect of levodopa.
warnings: Metoclopramide: FDA boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia with treatment beyond 12 weeks.
Domperidone: QT prolongation; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and in cardiac conduction disease.
Erythromycin: QT prolongation and CYP3A4 inhibition; tachyphylaxis limits it to short courses.
Metformin, omeprazole and acetaminophen: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
Aspirin allergy recorded: not relevant to the dopaminergic or prokinetic options.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Henderson is a 75-year-old right-handed retired professor who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Helen, for evaluation of progressive gait difficulty and generalized stiffness that has been worsening over the past twelve to fourteen months. His wife first noticed changes approximately a year ago when he began walking more slowly and appeared less steady on his feet, particularly when navigating around furniture or stepping off curbs. Over the ensuing months, he has developed bilateral stiffness that he describes as feeling like his arms and legs are heavy and resistant to movement, worse in the mornings and improving somewhat with activity. He has not noticed a clear resting tremor, though his wife reports that she has occasionally seen his left hand trembling slightly when he is sitting and watching television, which he attributes to fatigue. He has noticed that his handwriting has become smaller and more cramped over the past six months, and he has had increasing difficulty buttoning his shirt in the mornings. His voice has become quieter according to family members, though he himself is not aware of this change. He has had two near-falls in the past three months, both occurring when he attempted to turn quickly while walking, but he has not actually fallen. His wife reports that he has become somewhat slower in his movements overall, taking longer to get dressed, to eat meals, and to complete household tasks. She has also noted that his facial expression seems less animated than it used to be, and friends have commented that he looks tired or unwell even when he feels fine. He continues to drive short distances in their neighborhood but has voluntarily stopped driving on the highway due to feeling less confident. He denies any urinary incontinence, significant cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, or acting out of dreams. His appetite has been reduced, which his gastroenterologist attributes to his gastroparesis, and he has lost approximately eight pounds over the past year. He has been taking metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for the past three years for gastroparesis. He reports that his symptoms have progressed gradually over the past year despite being on a stable dose of metoclopramide.

neurological_exam.additional: No myoclonus. No fasciculations. Glabellar tap sign positive (Myerson sign). No vertical gaze palsy. No cerebellar ataxia. Handwriting sample shows mild micrographia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin mildly slow bilaterally but accurate. Rapid alternating movements mildly slowed bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial expression mildly hypomimic bilaterally, described as masked facies. Visual fields full to confrontation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait mildly slow with reduced arm swing bilaterally. Stride length mildly shortened. Mild difficulty with tandem gait. Slight unsteadiness on turns but no festination. Pull test shows two steps of retropulsion, recovers independently. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. MMSE 28/30, losing one point on delayed recall (2/3 at 5 minutes) and one point on pentagons copy. Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent with intact naming and repetition. No evidence of frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk mildly reduced in bilateral upper extremities. Mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity at the wrists, slightly more prominent on the left than the right. Mild bilateral bradykinesia on finger tapping and rapid alternating movements, with decrement in amplitude and speed bilaterally. No resting tremor observed during examination, though patient endorses occasional hand tremor. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact in all extremities. Vibration sense mildly decreased at bilateral great toes. Proprioception intact. Pinprick intact.
